statute_title: Driving Under the Influence of Alcohol or a Drug (DUI)
offense_class: Misdemeanor (all offenses; enhanced penalties for repeat)
elements: Defendant operated or was in physical control of a vehicle
In the District of Columbia
While under the influence of intoxicating liquor or any drug or combination
Or with a BAC of .08 or higher
enhancements: BAC .20 or higher (mandatory minimum 10 days first; 15 days second; 20 days third+)
BAC .25 or higher (mandatory minimum 15 days first; 20 days second; 25 days third+)
BAC .30 or higher (mandatory minimum 20 days first; 25 days second; 30 days third+)
Child under 18 in vehicle (additional penalties under § 50-2206.18)
Second offense within 15 years (5 days mandatory minimum)
Third+ offense within 15 years (10 days mandatory minimum)
notes: DC uses a tiered BAC system with escalating mandatory minimums. OWI (Operating While Impaired, § 50-2206.14) is a lesser offense. Implied consent under § 50-1904.02.

elements: Defendant operated or was in physical control of a vehicle
While under the influence of alcohol or drugs
BAC .08 or higher, or actual impairment
No prior DUI convictions within 15 years
mandatory_minimum: No mandatory minimum unless BAC .20+ (10 days); .25+ (15 days); .30+ (20 days)
notes: First offense without aggravating factors has no mandatory minimum. Diversion and treatment programs available. License revocation 6 months-1 year.

elements: Defendant operated or was in physical control of a vehicle
While under the influence of alcohol or drugs
BAC .08 or higher, or actual impairment
One or more prior DUI/OWI convictions within 15 years
mandatory_minimum: 5 days (second); 10 days (third+); increased with high BAC
notes: DC uses a 15-year lookback period. Third offense mandatory minimum is 10 days. License revocation 2+ years for repeat offenders.

offense_class: Same as alcohol DUI by offense count
penalty_max: Same as alcohol DUI by offense count
fine_max: Same as alcohol DUI by offense count
elements: Defendant operated or was in physical control of a vehicle
While under the influence of any drug or combination of alcohol and a drug
To a degree which renders the defendant incapable of safely operating the vehicle
mandatory_minimum: Same as alcohol DUI by offense count
enhancements: Combined influence of alcohol and drugs
notes: No per se drug limit in DC. Prosecution must prove actual impairment. DC decriminalized marijuana possession but DUI-drugs still applies.

elements: Defendant drove any vehicle in the District
In a manner that endangered the safety of persons or property
With willful disregard for safety
notes: Common plea-down from DUI. DC also has aggressive driving (§ 50-2201.04(b-1)) as a separate offense.

statute_title: Leaving After Colliding — Serious Bodily Injury or Death
offense_class: Felony (serious injury/death); Misdemeanor (property damage or minor injury)
elements: Defendant was the operator of a vehicle involved in a collision
Collision resulted in injury, death, or property damage
Defendant knowingly failed to stop and provide identification and assistance
notes: Leaving after colliding involving death carries up to 15 years. Property damage only is a misdemeanor under § 50-2201.05c(a).

statute_title: Aggravated Reckless Driving Resulting in Death
elements: Defendant operated a vehicle in the District
In a manner demonstrating extreme disregard for human life
Defendant's operation caused the death of another person
notes: DC does not have a specific vehicular homicide statute. Deaths caused by DUI may be charged under homicide statutes or aggravated reckless driving.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
Through criminal negligence or recklessness while operating a vehicle
notes: DC does not have a separate vehicular manslaughter statute. Vehicular deaths are prosecuted under general manslaughter provisions.

statute_title: Operating After Suspension or Revocation of License
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
While defendant's license was suspended or revoked
Defendant had knowledge of the suspension or revocation
notes: Driving on a DUI-related suspension carries additional penalties. Insurance-related suspension driving has lower penalties.

statute_title: Fleeing from a Law Enforcement Officer in a Motor Vehicle
elements: A law enforcement officer gave a visual or audible signal to stop
Defendant was operating a motor vehicle
Defendant knowingly failed to stop
Defendant attempted to flee or elude the officer
enhancements: Causing injury or death during flight
notes: Vehicular fleeing is always a felony in DC. Fleeing on foot from law enforcement is a separate misdemeanor.

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed a controlled substance
Without a valid prescription
Substance is listed in Schedules I through V
enhancements: PCP possession (felony — up to 3 years and $12,500 under § 48-904.01(d)(2))
notes: Simple possession is a misdemeanor except for PCP (which is a felony). First offenders eligible for conditional release — charges dismissed upon completion of probation. DC decriminalized marijuana possession under 2 oz in 2014.

fine_max: $25 civil fine (1-2 oz); criminal for 2+ oz
elements: Defendant possessed marijuana
Amount over 2 ounces for criminal charges
Under 2 ounces: civil fine only
notes: Initiative 71 (2015) legalized possession of up to 2 oz of marijuana for personal use by adults 21+. Growing up to 6 plants (3 mature) is legal. Sale remains illegal. Federal law still applies on federal property in DC.

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed cocaine
Cocaine is a Schedule II controlled substance
Without a valid prescription
notes: Simple cocaine possession is a misdemeanor. First offense eligible for conditional release. Possession with intent to distribute is a felony.

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed methamphetamine
Methamphetamine is a Schedule II controlled substance
Without a valid prescription
notes: Simple meth possession is a misdemeanor. Manufacturing methamphetamine is a felony under § 48-904.01(a).

statute_title: Manufacture or Distribution of Controlled Substance — Schedule I or II
elements: Defendant manufactured, distributed, or possessed with intent to distribute
A controlled substance classified in Schedule I or II
Including heroin, cocaine, fentanyl, PCP, or methamphetamine
enhancements: Second offense (twice the maximum — up to 60 years)
Third offense (three times maximum or life)
Distribution to a minor (additional penalties under § 48-904.06)
Within 1,000 feet of a school, park, or public housing (§ 48-904.07a)
notes: DC drug penalties are among the most severe in the country. Second offense doubles the maximum. Distribution near schools carries enhanced penalties.

statute_title: Distribution of Controlled Substance — Schedule III-V
penalty_max: 5 years (Schedule III); 3 years (Schedule IV); 1 year (Schedule V)
elements: Defendant distributed or possessed with intent to distribute
A controlled substance from Schedule III through V
notes: Schedule III includes anabolic steroids, ketamine. Schedule IV includes benzodiazepines. Schedule V includes codeine preparations.

penalty_max: 30 years (Schedule I-II); 5 years (Schedule III); 3 years (Schedule IV)
elements: Defendant manufactured a controlled substance
Through chemical synthesis or processing
notes: Manufacturing is prosecuted under the same statute as distribution. Clandestine lab operations carry additional cleanup and restitution costs.

elements: Defendant possessed drug paraphernalia
Knowing or intending it to be used for manufacturing, testing, or consuming a controlled substance
enhancements: Delivery of paraphernalia to a minor
notes: DC has relatively light penalties for paraphernalia possession. Marijuana paraphernalia for personal use by adults 21+ is legal under Initiative 71.

penalty_max: 30 years (Schedule I-II); 5 years (Schedule III); 3 years (Schedule IV)
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
With intent to distribute
Intent inferred from quantity, packaging, scales, cash, or communications
enhancements: Near school, park, or public housing (§ 48-904.07a)
notes: PWID carries the same penalties as distribution. Intent may be proven through circumstantial evidence.

penalty_max: Life imprisonment without possibility of release
elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
With premeditation and deliberate intent to kill
Or by means of poison or lying in wait
Or during the commission of certain enumerated felonies (felony murder)
mandatory_minimum: 30 years imprisonment (60 years if killing involved certain aggravating circumstances)
enhancements: Killing while lying in wait or by poison
notes: DC does not have the death penalty (abolished 1981). Minimum sentence is 30 years. Life without release is the maximum. Felony murder applies to killings during arson, robbery, sexual abuse, kidnapping, and burglary.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
With malice aforethought
Without premeditation or deliberation
notes: Second degree murder includes depraved heart murder — extreme recklessness demonstrating a depraved indifference to human life.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
Without malice
In the heat of passion upon adequate provocation
Or under circumstances that would reduce murder to manslaughter
notes: Voluntary manslaughter is an intentional killing mitigated by adequate provocation or heat of passion.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
Through criminal negligence or during commission of an unlawful act
notes: DC uses a single manslaughter statute covering both voluntary and involuntary. Sentencing depends on the circumstances.

elements: Defendant knowingly or purposely caused serious bodily injury to another person
Or assaulted another with a dangerous weapon
Or under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference to human life
enhancements: Use of a firearm (additional consecutive enhancement)
Against law enforcement officer, public official, or transit operator
notes: Aggravated assault is DC's most serious non-homicide assault. 'Serious bodily injury' includes risk of death, protracted loss of function, or serious disfigurement.

elements: Defendant unlawfully assaulted or threatened another person
In a menacing manner
notes: Simple assault is the base-level assault in DC. Covers both attempted battery and threatening behavior.

statute_title: Assault with Significant Bodily Injury (Felony Assault)
elements: Defendant unlawfully assaulted another person
And intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly caused significant bodily injury
notes: 'Significant bodily injury' includes injuries requiring hospitalization or medical treatment beyond what a layperson can administer, and lacerations requiring stitches.

elements: Defendant took property from the person or in the immediate presence of another
By force or violence or by putting the person in fear
enhancements: Against a senior citizen (additional 5 years under § 22-3601)
notes: Basic robbery carries a 2-year mandatory minimum. Armed robbery is separately charged under § 22-4502.

elements: Defendant committed robbery
While armed with or having readily available a pistol or other dangerous weapon
mandatory_minimum: 5 years additional consecutive sentence for armed enhancement
enhancements: Use of a firearm (additional 5 years mandatory consecutive under § 22-4502)
notes: DC's armed offense enhancement (§ 22-4502) adds a mandatory minimum 5-year consecutive sentence. Applies to robbery, assault, and other violent crimes committed while armed.

elements: Defendant seized, confined, or detained another person
Against that person's will
And held for ransom, reward, or used as a hostage
notes: Kidnapping carries up to 30 years. If not released within a reasonable time, the sentence may be enhanced.

elements: Defendant maliciously burned or attempted to burn a dwelling, building, or other property
notes: Burning a dwelling carries up to 15 years. Burning other property carries up to 10 years. Attempted arson carries up to 5 years.

penalty_max: Life imprisonment (if target is first degree murder)
elements: Defendant had specific intent to kill another person
Defendant performed an overt act toward committing murder
The murder was not completed
notes: DC does not reduce attempt penalties by one grade for serious offenses. Attempted murder may carry up to life imprisonment.

elements: Defendant assaulted another person
With a dangerous weapon
Including a firearm, knife, or any instrument capable of causing serious bodily injury
enhancements: While armed with firearm (additional 5 years consecutive under § 22-4502)
notes: ADW is one of the most commonly charged felonies in DC. The 'while armed' enhancement adds a mandatory 5-year consecutive sentence.

elements: Defendant obtained or used the property of another
With intent to deprive the owner
Value of property $1,000 or more
enhancements: From a senior citizen (additional 5 years under § 22-3601)
notes: First degree theft threshold is $1,000. Second degree (under $1,000) is a misdemeanor.

elements: Defendant obtained or used the property of another
With intent to deprive the owner of the right to or benefit of the property
Value of property $1,000 or more
notes: DC's felony theft threshold is $1,000.

elements: Defendant obtained or used the property of another
With intent to deprive the owner
Value of property less than $1,000
notes: Second degree theft is a misdemeanor for property under $1,000.

elements: Defendant willfully concealed or took possession of merchandise of a store
Without paying full purchase price
With intent to appropriate without payment
enhancements: Use of device to defeat security
notes: DC has a specific shoplifting statute. Retailers may also pursue civil recovery.

elements: Defendant entered or attempted to enter a building or dwelling
With intent to commit any criminal offense therein
notes: First degree burglary (§ 22-801(a)) is committed at night or while armed, or involves a dwelling — up to 30 years. Second degree is other burglary — up to 15 years.

elements: Defendant entered or attempted to enter a dwelling
With intent to commit any criminal offense therein
Nighttime entry or while armed
notes: First degree burglary applies to dwellings, nighttime entries, or entries while armed. Mandatory minimum 5 years.

statute_title: Unauthorized Use of a Motor Vehicle
elements: Defendant took, used, or operated a motor vehicle
Without the consent of the owner
Or aided in such taking
notes: DC uses 'unauthorized use of a vehicle' rather than motor vehicle theft. Always a felony regardless of vehicle value.

elements: Defendant received, retained, or disposed of property of another
Knowing or having reason to believe the property was stolen
notes: Penalty tiers mirror theft: $1,000 threshold divides felony from misdemeanor.

elements: Defendant maliciously injured or destroyed property of another
Or defaced property of another
notes: Felony threshold is $1,000 in damages. DC takes graffiti and defacement of public property seriously.

elements: Defendant entered or attempted to enter property of another
Against the will of the owner or lawful occupant
Or remained after being asked to leave
notes: DC uses 'unlawful entry' rather than 'trespass.' Includes entering posted property and refusing to leave when asked.

elements: Defendant maliciously injured, broke, or destroyed property of another
notes: DC uses 'destruction of property' rather than 'criminal mischief.' Same statute covers vandalism and reckless property damage.

elements: Defendant committed an intrafamily offense — assault against a family member, household member, or intimate partner
Family/household member includes spouse, former spouse, persons with child in common, roommates, or persons in a romantic relationship
notes: DC has an intrafamily offense designation that applies to any crime committed against a family/household member. Mandatory arrest policy. Civil protection orders under § 16-1005.

statute_title: Intrafamily Offense — Assault with Significant Bodily Injury
elements: Defendant assaulted a family or household member
And caused significant bodily injury
Intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly
notes: Felony domestic battery (significant bodily injury) carries up to 3 years. Aggravated assault enhancement available. Federal firearms prohibition applies.

elements: Defendant was a person responsible for a child's welfare
Defendant intentionally, knowingly, or negligently engaged in conduct
Creating a grave risk of bodily injury to the child
enhancements: First degree cruelty to children (intentional — up to 15 years under § 22-1101(a))
notes: First degree cruelty requires intentional, malicious conduct — up to 15 years. Second degree covers reckless or negligent endangerment.

elements: Defendant was a person responsible for a child's welfare
Defendant intentionally and maliciously tortured, beat, or otherwise maltreated a child
Under circumstances indicating an intent to cause serious harm
notes: First degree cruelty to children is the most serious child abuse charge. Covers intentional and malicious conduct.

statute_title: Violation of a Civil Protection Order
offense_class: Misdemeanor (first); may be held in contempt
elements: A valid civil protection order was in effect
Defendant had knowledge of the order
Defendant knowingly violated the order
notes: Violation of a CPO can be prosecuted criminally or held in contempt. Civil protection orders in DC cover domestic violence, stalking, and sexual abuse.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (first); Felony (with threat of serious bodily injury, or prior conviction)
elements: Defendant purposefully engaged in a course of conduct directed at a specific individual
With intent to cause that individual to fear for safety or suffer emotional distress
Or should have known the conduct would cause reasonable fear or distress
enhancements: In violation of a court order (felony)
notes: Misdemeanor stalking with a threat of serious bodily injury is elevated to felony. Course of conduct requires two or more acts.

elements: Defendant engaged in a course of conduct directed at another person
That would cause a reasonable person to feel frightened, intimidated, or emotionally distressed
And defendant should have known the conduct would cause such effects
notes: DC's stalking statute covers general harassment as misdemeanor stalking. Includes electronic and telephone harassment.

elements: Defendant caused physical injury to a vulnerable adult
Through an intentional or knowing act
Defendant was a caretaker or in a position of trust
notes: DC has specific statutes for vulnerable adult abuse, exploitation, and neglect. Financial exploitation of a vulnerable adult carries up to 10 years.

statute_title: Carrying a Pistol Without a License
elements: Defendant carried a pistol, machine gun, or sawed-off shotgun
Without a valid registration and license to carry
In the District of Columbia
enhancements: Carrying during commission of a crime of violence (additional 5 years consecutive under § 22-4502)
notes: DC has extremely strict gun laws. All firearms must be registered. Concealed carry licenses available but difficult to obtain. Federal buildings add federal jurisdiction.

statute_title: Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm
Defendant had previously been convicted of a felony
Or convicted of a crime of violence
enhancements: Possession during commission of a violent crime
notes: DC prohibits firearm possession by anyone convicted of a felony or crime of violence. Also prohibits possession by persons committed for mental health treatment.

statute_title: Carrying a Pistol Without a License
elements: Defendant carried a pistol or other prohibited weapon
Without a valid DC concealed carry license
Openly or concealed
notes: DC concealed carry license issued by MPD. Very restrictive — 'good reason' requirement was struck down but process remains strict. All firearms must be registered.

elements: Defendant discharged a firearm in the District of Columbia
In a manner that endangered the safety of any person
notes: Unlawful discharge is always a felony in DC. Separate from assault with a dangerous weapon charges.

elements: Defendant knowingly used personal identifying information of another
To obtain property or anything of value exceeding $1,000
Or affected 10 or more individual victims
notes: Second degree identity theft (under $1,000 or fewer victims) is a misdemeanor — 180 days and $1,000 fine.

elements: Defendant was entrusted with property of another
Defendant wrongfully obtained or used the property
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: DC does not have a separate embezzlement statute. Embezzlement is prosecuted as theft — wrongfully obtaining or using property of another.

elements: Defendant falsely made, completed, or altered a written instrument
With intent to defraud or deceive another person
notes: Written instruments include checks, deeds, contracts, public records, prescriptions. Uttering a forged instrument is included.

elements: Defendant engaged in a scheme or systematic course of conduct
With intent to defraud or obtain property of another through false pretenses
notes: DC fraud statute covers theft by deception, false pretenses, and scheme-based fraud.

elements: Defendant used a credit or debit card
Knowing it was stolen, forged, revoked, or canceled
Or used without the cardholder's authorization
notes: Multiple transactions aggregated for threshold purposes. Includes use of stolen card numbers for online purchases.

statute_number: D.C. Code § 22-1901; federal statutes often apply
elements: Defendant conducted a financial transaction involving criminally derived property
With knowledge that the property was proceeds of criminal activity
With intent to promote or conceal the criminal activity
notes: Money laundering in DC is often prosecuted federally due to the unique federal jurisdiction in the District. Federal penalties are significantly higher.

elements: Defendant engaged in a sexual act with another person
By using threats that would place a reasonable person in fear of harm
Or when defendant knew or should have known the person was incapable of consent
notes: DC uses 'sexual abuse' rather than 'sexual assault' or 'rape.' First degree (§ 22-3002) applies when force or threats of death are used — up to life. Sex offender registration required.

elements: Defendant engaged in a sexual act with another person
By using force or threat of death, serious bodily injury, or kidnapping
Or by rendering the victim unconscious
Or by administering a drug without consent
notes: DC uses 'sexual abuse' rather than 'rape.' First degree sexual abuse is the most serious — carries up to life imprisonment. Sex offender registration required.

elements: Defendant made an obscene or indecent exposure of person
In a public place or in view of the public
enhancements: In the presence of a minor
notes: Repeat offenses or exposure involving minors may trigger sex offender registration.

statute_title: Engaging in Prostitution / Soliciting for Prostitution
elements: Defendant offered or agreed to engage in sexual activity
For a fee or thing of value
enhancements: Third or subsequent offense (up to 2 years)
notes: DC decriminalized consensual sex work for the seller in some contexts but buyers and traffickers still face prosecution. Promoting prostitution (§ 22-2710) is a felony.

elements: Defendant employed, used, or permitted a minor to engage in a sexual performance
Knowing the character and content of the performance
notes: Possession of child pornography (§ 22-3102) is also a felony. Distribution carries enhanced penalties.

statute_title: Failure to Register as a Sex Offender
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender
Defendant knowingly failed to register or update registration
notes: Registration requirements under the Sex Offender Registration Act of 1999. Must register within 3 days of release or relocation to DC.

elements: Defendant engaged in a sexual act or sexual contact with a child
First degree: victim under 12
Second degree: victim 12-15, defendant 4+ years older
enhancements: Victim under 12 (first degree — up to life)
notes: DC's age of consent is 16. Child sexual abuse covers sexual acts with persons under 16. First degree (under 12) carries up to life.

elements: Defendant engaged in loud, threatening, or tumultuous behavior
In a public place
With intent to provoke a breach of the peace or under circumstances creating a risk thereof
notes: General catch-all for public disturbances. First Amendment protections limit application to speech and protests.

elements: A law enforcement officer was making a lawful arrest
Defendant knowingly resisted, opposed, or interfered with the arrest
By means of force or violence
enhancements: Causing injury to officer (separate assault charge)
notes: Resisting arrest requires physical resistance. Verbal protests alone are not sufficient. Separate from obstruction.

elements: Defendant knowingly obstructed, impeded, or attempted to obstruct
A pending or anticipated official proceeding
By means of bribery, misrepresentation, intimidation, force, or threats
notes: Obstruction of justice in DC is always a felony. Includes witness tampering, evidence destruction, and interference with official proceedings.

elements: Defendant willfully disobeyed a lawful court order
Or engaged in disruptive conduct in court
notes: DC Superior Court and US District Court both have contempt authority. Federal contempt power applies on federal property.

offense_class: Not a criminal offense in DC
elements: Person is intoxicated in a public place
And is a danger to self or others
notes: DC decriminalized public intoxication. Intoxicated persons are taken to a sobering station or treatment facility, not jail. Disorderly conduct may be charged if behavior is disruptive.

offense_class: Felony (if underlying is felony); Misdemeanor (if underlying is misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant was released pending trial or pending appeal
Defendant willfully failed to appear as required by the court
notes: Bail jumping severity matches the underlying charge. DC Pretrial Services Agency supervises released defendants.

elements: Defendant knowingly made a false statement
To a law enforcement officer
Regarding the commission of a crime
notes: Filing a false report of a crime is a misdemeanor. False bomb threats or emergency reports carry enhanced penalties.

elements: Defendant knowingly and purposely made a threat to injure another person
Or threatened to damage property of another
Under circumstances creating a reasonable fear
enhancements: Threat to a public official or law enforcement officer (enhanced)
notes: Threats to kidnap or injure persons are misdemeanors. Threats involving weapons may be charged as assault with a dangerous weapon.

elements: Defendant made a false material statement
Under oath in a judicial or official proceeding
Knowing the statement was false
notes: Subornation of perjury carries the same penalties. False statements to federal agencies may be prosecuted under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.

elements: Defendant offered, gave, or promised something of value
To a public official or public employee
With intent to influence the official's action or decision
notes: Federal bribery statutes (18 U.S.C. § 201) may also apply given DC's unique federal jurisdiction. Receiving a bribe carries the same penalties.

elements: Defendant was lawfully in custody or confined
Defendant escaped from custody or a correctional institution
enhancements: Use of force or violence during escape
notes: Escape sentence runs consecutive to original sentence. DC inmates are held in BOP facilities — federal escape charges may also apply.

elements: Defendant knowingly and intentionally tortured, beat, or cruelly treated an animal
Or caused unnecessary suffering
enhancements: Aggravated cruelty — torture or killing (felony — up to 5 years)
notes: DC has strong animal cruelty laws. Aggravated cruelty involving torture or killing is a felony. Animal fighting is a separate felony.

offense_class: Varies — court may revoke probation and impose original sentence
elements: Defendant was placed on probation by DC Superior Court
Defendant violated a condition of probation
notes: Court has discretion to modify, extend, or revoke probation. Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency (CSOSA) supervises DC probationers.

offense_class: Varies — return to prison for remaining term
elements: Defendant was released on parole or supervised release
Defendant violated a condition of release
notes: DC parole is supervised by the US Parole Commission. DC inmates serve sentences in BOP facilities. Supervised release violations are heard by US Parole Commission.

elements: Defendant aided, abetted, counseled, or encouraged another person
In the commission of a crime
With knowledge of the criminal plan and intent to facilitate it
notes: All parties to a crime are equally liable. Mere presence is not sufficient — must show intentional participation.

offense_class: Same as the completed offense (DC does not automatically reduce for attempts)
elements: Defendant had intent to commit a specific crime
Defendant took a substantial step toward its commission
The crime was not completed
notes: DC does not statutorily reduce penalties for attempts — the court has discretion. Attempt to commit a crime carries the same maximum as the completed offense.

offense_class: Same as target offense (maximum same as object offense)
elements: Two or more persons agreed to commit a crime
An overt act was performed in furtherance of the conspiracy
notes: Conspiracy penalties mirror the target offense. Co-conspirators liable for all reasonably foreseeable acts in furtherance of the conspiracy.
